monitored_text: Resources / Materials / 6 Types of Synthetic Polymers 6 Types of Synthetic Polymers Written by Megan Conniff Updated by Audrius Zidonis PhD 28 min read Published November 25, 2026 The 6 types of synthetic polymers are thermoplastics, thermosetting polymers (thermosets), elastomers, synthetic fibers, biodegradable synthetic polymers, and engineering plastics, each classified by molecular structure, thermal behavior, and mechanical performance. Synthetic polymers are large-chain molecules produced through polymerization of monomer units derived from petrochemical feedstocks, engineered to deliver specific physical and chemical properties across industrial and consumer applications. Thermoplastics (polyethylene and polypropylene) soften upon heating and resolidify upon cooling, while thermosets (epoxy and phenolic resins) cure irreversibly through cross-linking. Elastomers (silicone and styrene-butadiene rubber) exhibit high elastic recovery, and synthetic fibers (nylon and polyester) provide tensile strength in textile applications. Biodegradable synthetic polymers (polylactic acid and polyglycolic acid) are engineered to decompose under specific environmental conditions, addressing sustainability demands in packaging and medical applications. Engineering plastics (polycarbonate and polyamide) deliver superior mechanical and thermal performance compared to commodity plastics, making them suitable for structural and load-bearing applications. The six polymer types span a tensile strength range from 10 MPa in soft elastomers to over 100 MPa in engineering plastics, reflecting the broad mechanical spectrum covered by synthetic polymer materials across manufacturing, construction, medical, and consumer product industries. 1. Thermoplastics Thermoplastics are synthetic polymers that soften when heated and resolidify upon cooling, allowing repeated reshaping without chemical degradation of the polymer chain. The types of thermoplastics are polyethylene (PE), polypropylene (PP), polyvinyl chloride (PVC), polystyrene (PS), polyethylene terephthalate (PET), nylon, and acrylic (PMMA), each differentiated by molecular structure, thermal behavior, and mechanical performance. Thermoplastics are processed through injection molding, extrusion, and thermoforming at temperatures ranging from 150°C to 350°C, depending on polymer type and grade. The absence of cross-linking in thermoplastic molecular chains allows the material to be remelted and reprocessed multiple times without property loss. Thermoplastics achieve tensile strength from 15 MPa in low-density polyethylene (LDPE) to over 80 MPa in nylon and engineering-grade acrylic (PMMA). The softening point, measured as the heat deflection temperature (HDT), ranges from 50°C in low-density polyethylene to 140°C in polypropylene homopolymer grades. The combination of processability, mechanical versatility, and recyclability positions thermoplastics as the most widely produced synthetic polymer category, accounting for approximately 80% of global plastic production, reinforcing their widespread role as a thermoplastic manufacturing material . Polyethylene (PE) Polyethylene is the most produced thermoplastic, synthesized through the polymerization of ethylene monomers (C₂H₄) into long-chain molecular structures ranging from low-density (LDPE) to high-density (HDPE) grades. LDPE achieves tensile strength from 8 MPa to 20 MPa, while HDPE reaches 21 MPa to 37 MPa. LDPE is characterized by a branched molecular structure that reduces crystallinity to 45% to 55%, producing a flexible, transparent film material. HDPE exhibits a linear molecular structure with crystallinity from 70% to 90%, generating a stiffer, more rigid material suitable for structural applications. LDPE is used in packaging films, squeeze bottles, and agricultural sheeting, while HDPE is applied in pipes, containers, and industrial tanks. Polyethylene resists moisture, dilute acids, and alkalis, maintaining chemical stability across a broad range of industrial and consumer Polyethylene (PE) applications. Polypropylene (PP) Polypropylene is a semi-crystalline thermoplastic produced through the polymerization of propylene monomers (C₃H₆), achieving tensile strength from 25 MPa to 40 MPa and a heat deflection temperature from 100°C to 140°C. The polymer is produced in three primary tacticity forms (isotactic, syndiotactic, and atactic), with isotactic polypropylene accounting for the dominant share of commercial production due to its superior stiffness and thermal resistance. Polypropylene density ranges from 0.895 g/cm³ to 0.92 g/cm³, making it the lightest commodity thermoplastic in commercial production. Its fatigue resistance makes it the preferred material for living hinges, withstanding over 1,000,000 flex cycles without fracture. Polypropylene is applied in automotive components, food packaging containers, medical devices, and textile fiber production, where chemical resistance and thermal stability define the performance range of Polypropylene (PP) . Polyvinyl Chloride (PVC) Polyvinyl chloride is a thermoplastic produced through the polymerization of vinyl chloride monomers (C₂H₃Cl), available in rigid and flexible formulations with tensile strength from 40 MPa to 60 MPa in rigid grades. Rigid PVC (uPVC) contains no plasticizer additives, producing a stiff material with a density of 1.3 g/cm³ to 1.45 g/cm³ used in pipe systems, window profiles, and building cladding. Flexible PVC is produced through the addition of plasticizers (dioctyl phthalate or diisononyl phthalate) at concentrations from 10% to 60% by weight, reducing stiffness for cable insulation, flooring, and medical tubing applications. PVC achieves a limiting oxygen index (LOI) from 45% to 49%, classifying it as a self-extinguishing material with inherent flame resistance. The rigid and flexible formulation range defines the broad industrial applicability of Polyvinyl Chloride (PVC) . Polystyrene (PS) Polystyrene is an amorphous thermoplastic produced through the polymerization of styrene monomers (C₈H₈), achieving tensile strength from 25 MPa to 50 MPa in standard grades and up to 55 MPa in high-impact polystyrene (HIPS). Standard polystyrene exhibits a glass transition temperature of approximately 100°C, above which the material softens and loses structural rigidity. HIPS is produced by incorporating polybutadiene rubber into the polystyrene matrix at concentrations from 5% to 15%, increasing impact resistance at the cost of optical clarity. Expanded polystyrene (EPS) is produced by introducing a blowing agent during polymerization, generating a closed-cell foam structure with densities from 10 kg/m³ to 50 kg/m³ for thermal insulation applications. The range of standard, high-impact, and expanded grades defines the broad application spectrum of Polystyrene (PS) . Polyethylene Terephthalate (PET) Polyethylene terephthalate is a semi-crystalline thermoplastic polyester produced through the condensation polymerization of ethylene glycol and terephthalic acid, achieving tensile strength from 50 MPa to 80 MPa. The crystallinity of PET ranges from 0% in amorphous grades to 60% in highly oriented fiber grades, with crystallinity directly influencing mechanical strength and barrier performance. PET exhibits an oxygen permeability from 0.05 to 0.1 cm³·mm/(m²·day·atm), making it the preferred barrier material for carbonated beverage bottles and food packaging. The intrinsic viscosity of PET, measured from 0.55 dL/g to 0.85 dL/g, determines suitability for bottle, film, or fiber applications, with higher viscosity grades used in structural fiber production. The barrier performance and mechanical range of PET define the material versatility of Polyethylene Terephthalate (PET) across the packaging and textile industries. Nylon Nylon is a semi-crystalline polyamide thermoplastic produced through condensation polymerization, achieving tensile strength from 50 MPa to 85 MPa and a melting point from 215°C to 265°C, depending on grade. Nylon 6 is produced through ring-opening polymerization of caprolactam, while Nylon 6,6 is synthesized through the condensation of hexamethylenediamine and adipic acid, producing a polymer with slightly higher stiffness and thermal resistance. The moisture absorption of nylon ranges from 1.5% to 3.5% at equilibrium, reducing tensile strength and dimensional stability in high-humidity environments. Nylon exhibits a coefficient of friction from 0.15 to 0.40 against steel, making it suitable for self-lubricating gear, bearing, and bushing applications without external lubrication. The wear resistance and fatigue strength of nylon grades define the mechanical performance range of Nylon Types across industrial and textile applications. Acrylic (PMMA) Acrylic, or polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA), is an amorphous thermoplastic produced through the polymerization of methyl methacrylate monomers (C₅H₈O₂), achieving tensile strength from 50 MPa to 75 MPa and light transmittance of approximately 92%. The glass transition temperature of PMMA ranges from 85°C to 105°C, above which the material softens sufficiently for thermoforming and reshaping operations. PMMA exhibits a Vickers hardness from 18 HV to 20 HV, providing superior scratch resistance compared to polycarbonate at 14 HV to 16 HV. The refractive index of PMMA measures 1.49, closely matching optical glass and making it suitable for precision optical lenses, light guides, and display panel applications. The optical clarity, UV resistance, and dimensional stability of PMMA define the performance characteristics of Acrylic (PMMA) across signage, glazing, and medical device applications. 2. Thermosetting Polymers (Thermosets) Thermosetting polymers are synthetic polymers that harden permanently after heating through an irreversible cross-linking reaction, forming a rigid three-dimensional molecular network that cannot be remelted or reshaped after curing. The types of thermosetting polymers are thermosetting epoxy resins, phenolic resins (Bakelite), melamine formaldehyde, urea formaldehyde, and polyester resins, each differentiated by curing mechanism, cross-link density, and mechanical performance. Thermosets are processed through compression molding, transfer molding, and resin infusion at curing temperatures from 120°C to 200°C, depending on resin system and hardener composition. The irreversible cross-linked network prevents molecular chain movement above the glass transition temperature, producing a dimensionally stable material that retains structural integrity under sustained thermal and mechanical loading. Thermosets achieve tensile strength from 40 MPa in urea formaldehyde to over 130 MPa in high-performance epoxy systems reinforced with carbon or glass fiber. The heat deflection temperature of thermosets ranges from 130°C in polyester resins to over 250°C in high-temperature epoxy formulations. The permanent cross-linked structure, thermal stability, and chemical resistance of thermosets position them as the preferred polymer class for structural composites, electrical insulation, and high-temperature industrial applications, defining the core performance attributes of Thermosetting Polymers (Thermosets) . Epoxy Resins Epoxy resins are thermosetting polymers produced through the reaction of epichlorohydrin and bisphenol-A (BPA), forming a polymer with reactive epoxide groups that cure irreversibly upon exposure to hardeners (amines, anhydrides, or polyamides) at temperatures from 20°C to 200°C. The cured epoxy network achieves tensile strength from 55 MPa to 130 MPa, compressive strength from 100 MPa to 200 MPa, and a glass transition temperature from 120°C to 180°C, depending on hardener type and curing conditions. Epoxy resins exhibit excellent adhesion to metals, ceramics, and composite substrates, with bond shear strength from 10 MPa to 30 MPa in structural adhesive applications. The low shrinkage during curing, from 1% to 5% by volume, maintains dimensional accuracy in precision composite and tooling applications. The mechanical strength, chemical resistance, and adhesion performance define the broad industrial range of the epoxy definition . Phenolic Resins (Bakelite) Phenolic resins are thermosetting polymers produced through the condensation reaction of phenol and formaldehyde, forming a rigid cross-linked network that cures irreversibly under heat and pressure at temperatures from 150°C to 180°C. Bakelite, the first commercially produced synthetic polymer, introduced in 1907 by Leo Baekeland, remains the most recognized phenolic resin grade in industrial and consumer product history. Cured phenolic resins achieve tensile strength from 40 MPa to 70 MPa, compressive strength from 140 MPa to 210 MPa, and a heat deflection temperature from 150°C to 300°C, providing superior thermal stability among commodity thermosets. Phenolic resins exhibit a limiting oxygen index (LOI) from 25% to 35%, classifying them as inherently flame-resistant materials suitable for electrical components and fire-rated construction panels. The thermal stability and flame resistance define the industrial performance of phenolic resins . Melamine Formaldehyde Melamine formaldehyde is a thermosetting polymer produced through the condensation reaction of melamine and formaldehyde, forming a hard, rigid cross-linked network with superior surface hardness and scratch resistance compared to other amino resins. The cured polymer achieves tensile strength from 50 MPa to 80 MPa, compressive strength from 200 MPa to 300 MPa, and a heat deflection temperature from 130°C to 200°C, maintaining structural integrity under sustained thermal loading. Melamine formaldehyde exhibits a Brinell hardness from 25 HB to 40 HB, producing a surface resistant to abrasion, staining, and moisture penetration in decorative laminate and tableware applications. The material resists dilute acids and alkalis, maintaining surface integrity across food contact and chemical exposure conditions. Melamine formaldehyde is applied in decorative laminates, kitchenware, electrical components, and fire-retardant coatings across consumer and industrial product manufacturing. Urea Formaldehyde Urea formaldehyde is a thermosetting polymer produced through the condensation reaction of urea and formaldehyde, forming a rigid, colorless cross-linked network cured at temperatures from 100°C to 150°C under pressure. The cured polymer achieves tensile strength from 38 MPa to 55 MPa, compressive strength from 170 MPa to 230 MPa, and a heat deflection temperature from 120°C to 145°C, providing moderate thermal resistance for indoor applications. Urea formaldehyde exhibits superior hardness and surface finish quality, making it a preferred binder resin in particleboard, medium-density fiberboard (MDF), and decorative paper laminates at resin loading levels from 8% to 15% by weight. The material is susceptible to hydrolysis under prolonged moisture exposure, limiting its application to interior environments. Urea formaldehyde is applied in wood adhesives, electrical switch housings, and molded consumer product components. Polyester Resins Polyester resins are thermosetting polymers produced through the condensation polymerization of diols and dicarboxylic acids, dissolved in styrene monomer at concentrations from 30% to 50% by weight to form a liquid resin system that cures through free-radical cross-linking at room temperature or elevated temperatures. Unsaturated polyester resins (UPR) achieve tensile strength from 40 MPa to 90 MPa and a glass transition temperature from 70°C to 120°C, depending on resin formulation and reinforcement type. Orthophthalic polyester resins portray the standard grade, while isophthalic polyester resins provide superior corrosion resistance and mechanical performance for marine and chemical processing applications. Polyester resins exhibit volumetric shrinkage from 4% to 8% during curing, requiring careful mold design to maintain dimensional accuracy in composite part production. The cost-effectiveness and processing versatility define the broad application range of polyester definition across marine, automotive, and construction composite manufacturing. 3. Elastomers Elastomers are flexible, rubber-like synthetic polymers that stretch under applied force and return to their original shape upon load removal, a property governed by a lightly cross-linked molecular network that allows large reversible deformation. The types of elastomers are natural rubber, synthetic rubber, neoprene, silicone rubber, and polyurethane elastomers, each differentiated by chemical composition, cross-link density, and mechanical recovery performance. Elastomers are processed through vulcanization, compression molding, and extrusion at temperatures from 140°C to 200°C, with cross-link density controlling the balance between elastic recovery and stiffness across different grades. The elongation at break of elastomers ranges from 100% to over 800%, reflecting the exceptionally high deformation capacity that distinguishes them from rigid thermoplastics and thermosets. Elastomers achieve tensile strength from 10 MPa in standard synthetic rubber to 30 MPa in high-performance silicone and polyurethane grades. The service temperature range spans from 60°C in low-temperature silicone grades to 230°C in high-temperature silicone formulations, positioning elastomers as the preferred polymer class for sealing, cushioning, and flexible mechanical applications across industrial and consumer product manufacturing. Natural Rubber Natural rubber is an elastomer derived from the latex sap of the Hevea brasiliensis tree, composed of cis-1,4-polyisoprene chains with a molecular weight ranging from 100,000 g/mol to 1,000,000 g/mol. The raw latex is harvested through bark tapping, then processed through coagulation, drying, and vulcanization using sulfur at concentrations from 1% to 3% by weight to form cross-linked networks that improve mechanical performance. Vulcanized natural rubber achieves tensile strength from 25 MPa to 35 MPa, elongation at break from 500% to 800%, and a service temperature range from -50°C to 80°C. Natural rubber exhibits superior resilience and low heat buildup under dynamic loading, making it the preferred elastomer for high-performance tire treads, industrial conveyor belts, and vibration isolation mounts requiring consistent elastic recovery, defining its role as a foundational natural rubber elastomer material. Synthetic Rubber Synthetic rubber is a petrochemical-derived elastomer produced through the polymerization of monomers (styrene, butadiene, isoprene, and chloroprene) to replicate and extend the mechanical properties of natural rubber across industrial applications. Styrene-butadiene rubber (SBR), the most widely produced synthetic rubber grade, is composed of 23% to 25% styrene and 75% to 77% butadiene by weight, achieving tensile strength from 15 MPa to 25 MPa in carbon-black reinforced compounds. Synthetic rubber exhibits superior aging resistance, ozone resistance, and chemical stability compared to natural rubber, extending service life in outdoor and chemically aggressive environments. The service temperature range of synthetic rubber grades spans from -50°C to 120°C, depending on polymer type and compounding formulation. Synthetic rubber is applied in tire treads, conveyor belts, seals, hoses, and industrial gaskets, reinforcing its dominance as a synthetic rubber elastomer across high-volume manufacturing. Neoprene Neoprene is a synthetic elastomer produced through the free-radical polymerization of chloroprene monomers (C₄H₅Cl), forming a polychloroprene polymer with a chlorine content of approximately 40% by weight that provides inherent flame and chemical resistance. Vulcanized neoprene achieves tensile strength from 15 MPa to 25 MPa, elongation at break from 300% to 600%, and a service temperature range from -40°C to 120°C, maintaining flexibility across wide thermal fluctuations. Neoprene exhibits superior resistance to oils, ozone, weathering, and moderate concentrations of acids and alkalis, outperforming natural rubber in chemically aggressive environments. The flame resistance of neoprene, with a limiting oxygen index (LOI) from 26% to 28%, makes it preferable for cable jacketing and fire-rated sealing applications. The chemical resistance and thermal stability of neoprene distinguish it from silicone rubber in the silicone vs. neoprene elastomer comparison. Silicone Rubber Silicone rubber is an inorganic-organic elastomer produced through the polymerization of siloxane monomers (Si-O backbone), forming a polymer chain with methyl, vinyl, or phenyl side groups that govern thermal stability and mechanical performance across a service temperature range from -60°C to 230°C. Vulcanized silicone rubber achieves tensile strength from 5 MPa to 14 MPa, elongation at break from 100% to 700%, and a Shore A hardness from 10 to 80, depending on formulation and cross-link density. Silicone rubber exhibits superior biocompatibility, electrical insulation, and UV resistance compared to organic elastomers, maintaining mechanical properties across repeated thermal cycling. The dielectric strength of silicone rubber ranges from 15 kV/mm to 25 kV/mm, making it the preferred elastomer for high-voltage electrical insulation and medical implant applications, defining the performance scope of silicone rubber . Polyurethane Elastomers Polyurethane elastomers are synthetic elastomers produced through the reaction of polyols and diisocyanates, forming a segmented block copolymer structure with alternating hard and soft segments that govern mechanical performance and elastic recovery. Otto Bayer first synthesized polyurethane in 1937 at IG Farben laboratories in Germany, establishing the foundation for a polymer class that expanded into elastomers, foams, and coatings across industrial and consumer applications. Polyurethane elastomers achieve tensile strength from 20 MPa to 70 MPa, elongation at break from 300% to 600%, and Shore A hardness from 40 to 98, providing a broader mechanical range than natural rubber or neoprene. The abrasion resistance of polyurethane elastomers exceeds that of natural rubber by 3 to 5 times under standardized DIN 53516 testing conditions. The mechanical range and abrasion resistance define the industrial applications of polyurethane history across wheels, seals, and mining equipment components. 4. Synthetic Fibers Synthetic fibers are strong, lightweight polymer strands produced through the extrusion of petrochemical-derived polymer solutions or melts through spinnerets, engineered to deliver specific tensile, thermal, and moisture management properties across textile and industrial applications. The types of synthetic fibers are nylon, polyester, acrylic fiber, spandex (Lycra), and rayon (semi-synthetic), each differentiated by polymer composition, fiber structure, and performance characteristics in apparel, home textiles, and technical fabric applications. Synthetic fibers are produced through melt spinning, wet spinning, or dry spinning processes at extrusion temperatures from 220°C to 290°C, depending on polymer type and target fiber denier. The tenacity of synthetic fibers ranges from 2 grams per denier (g/d) in standard acrylic to over 9 g/d in high-tenacity polyester and nylon grades. Synthetic fibers achieve moisture regain values from 0.4% in polyester to 4.5% in nylon, directly influencing drying performance and comfort in apparel applications. The tensile strength of synthetic fiber yarns ranges from 300 MPa in standard acrylic to over 1,000 MPa in high-tenacity nylon and polyester industrial grades. The combination of lightweight structure, tensile performance, and processing versatility positions synthetic fibers as the dominant material class in global textile production, accounting for approximately 65% of total fiber output, reinforcing their role as the primary synthetic fibers in modern textile manufacturing. Nylon Nylon is a semi-crystalline polyamide synthetic fiber produced through condensation polymerization, achieving tenacity from 4 g/d to 9 g/d in standard and high-tenacity grades with a melting point from 215°C to 265°C depending on polymer type. Nylon 6 is produced through ring-opening polymerization of caprolactam, while Nylon 6,6 is synthesized through the condensation of hexamethylenediamine and adipic acid, producing a fiber with slightly higher tensile strength and thermal resistance. The moisture regain of nylon ranges from 3.5% to 4.5% at standard atmospheric conditions, providing better moisture management than polyester at 0.4% regain. Nylon fiber exhibits a coefficient of friction from 0.15 to 0.40 against standard surfaces, contributing to its durability in hosiery, activewear, and industrial textile applications. The tenacity range and abrasion resistance define the performance scope of nylon types across apparel and technical textile markets. Polyester Polyester is a semi-crystalline synthetic fiber produced through the condensation polymerization of ethylene glycol and terephthalic acid, forming polyethylene terephthalate (PET) fiber with tenacity from 3.5 g/d to 9.5 g/d in standard and high-tenacity grades. The moisture regain of polyester fiber is approximately 0.4% under standard atmospheric conditions, resulting in fast-drying performance in sportswear, outdoor apparel, and technical textile applications. Polyester fiber exhibits a melting point from 250°C to 265°C and a glass transition temperature from 70°C to 80°C, maintaining dimensional stability under repeated laundering at temperatures up to 60°C. The fiber resists stretching, shrinkage, and most mineral acids, maintaining tensile integrity across prolonged mechanical and chemical exposure. Polyester accounts for approximately 54% of global fiber production, making it the most widely manufactured synthetic fiber across apparel, home textiles, and industrial fabric applications. Acrylic Fiber Acrylic fiber is a synthetic textile fiber produced from polyacrylonitrile (PAN), a polymer composed of at least 85% acrylonitrile monomer by weight as defined by the U.S. Federal Trade Commission, with the remaining composition consisting of co-monomers (vinyl acetate or methyl acrylate) at concentrations from 5% to 15%. The fiber achieves tenacity from 2 g/d to 3.5 g/d, with a moisture regain of 1% to 2% at standard atmospheric conditions, enabling faster drying performance compared to wool at 17% moisture regain. Acrylic fiber density measures 1.17 g/cm³ to 1.18 g/cm³, placing it among the lightest synthetic fibers in commercial textile production. The crimped fiber structure traps air within the textile matrix, generating thermal insulation comparable to wool at lower fiber weight. The lightweight structure and wool-like thermal performance define the application range of acrylic fiber across cold-weather apparel and home textile markets. Spandex (Lycra) Spandex, marketed under the trade name Lycra, is a synthetic elastomeric fiber produced from segmented polyurethane polymer chains composed of alternating hard and soft segments, achieving elongation at break from 400% to 700% with full elastic recovery upon load removal. The fiber is produced through dry spinning of dimethylformamide (DMF) dissolved polyurethane solution at extrusion temperatures from 120°C to 180°C, forming continuous filaments at deniers from 10 to 2,500 depending on application requirements. Spandex achieves tenacity from 0.6 g/d to 0.9 g/d, lower than nylon or polyester, but delivers unmatched elastic recovery performance across repeated stretch cycles. The moisture regain of spandex measures approximately 1.3% at standard conditions, limiting its moisture management capacity in high-intensity athletic applications. Spandex is applied in swimwear, activewear, shapewear, and compression garments where stretch recovery from 400% to 700% is required. Rayon (Semi-synthetic) Rayon is a semi-synthetic fiber produced from regenerated cellulose derived from wood pulp or cotton linters, processed through chemical dissolution and wet spinning to form a fiber that bridges natural and fully synthetic textile materials. The cellulose source is dissolved in sodium hydroxide and carbon disulfide to form a viscose solution, then extruded through spinnerets into an acid coagulation bath at sulfuric acid concentrations from 10% to 15%, regenerating cellulose as continuous filaments. Rayon achieves tenacity from 1.5 g/d to 3.0 g/d in standard viscose grades and up to 6.9 g/d in high-tenacity modal and lyocell variants. The moisture regain of rayon ranges from 11% to 13% at standard atmospheric conditions, exceeding cotton at 8% and producing a highly absorbent, breathable fiber suitable for apparel and hygiene product applications. Rayon is applied in apparel linings, medical dressings, and nonwoven hygiene fabrics across consumer and industrial textile markets. 5. Biodegradable Synthetic Polymers Biodegradable synthetic polymers are engineered polymer materials that break down through microbial activity, hydrolysis, or enzymatic degradation under specific environmental conditions, reducing long-term plastic accumulation in landfills and marine environments. The types of biodegradable synthetic polymers are polylactic acid (PLA), polycaprolactone (PCL), and polybutylene succinate (PBS), each differentiated by degradation rate, mechanical performance, and target application. Biodegradable synthetic polymers are processed through injection molding, extrusion, and film blowing at temperatures from 150°C to 220°C, depending on polymer type and molecular weight. Tensile strength ranges from 20 MPa in flexible PCL grades to 60 MPa in rigid PLA formulations, covering a mechanical range suitable for packaging, medical, and agricultural film applications. The glass transition temperature spans from 60°C in PCL to 60°C in standard PLA grades, reflecting the broad thermal performance spectrum across the polymer class. The degradation rate ranges from 6 months under industrial composting conditions to years in ambient soil environments, positioning biodegradable synthetic polymers as a growing material class in sustainable packaging and medical device manufacturing. Polylactic Acid (PLA) Polylactic acid is a biodegradable thermoplastic polyester produced through the ring-opening polymerization of lactide, a cyclic diester derived from lactic acid fermentation of renewable carbohydrate sources (corn starch, sugarcane, and cassava). PLA achieves tensile strength from 50 MPa to 70 MPa, a glass transition temperature from 55°C to 60°C, and a melting point from 150°C to 180°C, providing mechanical properties comparable to polystyrene in rigid packaging applications. The biodegradation rate of PLA reaches 60% to 80% decomposition within 60 to 90 days under industrial composting conditions at temperatures above 58°C and relative humidity above 50%. PLA exhibits a molecular weight from 100,000 g/mol to 300,000 g/mol, directly influencing mechanical strength and processing behavior during extrusion and injection molding. The renewable feedstock origin and compostability define the sustainability profile of Polylactic Acid (PLA) across packaging, medical implant, and agricultural film applications. Polycaprolactone (PCL) Polycaprolactone is a biodegradable semi-crystalline polyester produced through the ring-opening polymerization of ε-caprolactone monomer, forming a flexible, low-melting polymer with a melting point from 59°C to 64°C and a glass transition temperature of approximately -60°C. PCL achieves tensile strength from 20 MPa to 42 MPa and elongation at break from 300% to 1,000%, providing exceptional flexibility compared to rigid biodegradable polymers (PLA and PBS). The biodegradation rate of PCL is slower than that of PLA, requiring 2 to 4 years for complete degradation in soil environments through hydrolytic and enzymatic chain scission. PCL molecular weight ranges from 10,000 g/mol to 100,000 g/mol, with higher molecular weight grades delivering greater mechanical strength and slower degradation rates. The flexibility, biocompatibility, and controlled degradation rate define the medical and tissue engineering applications of Polycaprolactone (PCL) in sutures, drug delivery systems, and scaffold fabrication. Polybutylene Succinate (PBS) Polybutylene succinate is a biodegradable semi-crystalline aliphatic polyester produced through the condensation polymerization of succinic acid and 1,4-butanediol, forming a thermoplastic polymer with a melting point from 113°C to 115°C and a glass transition temperature of approximately -32°C. PBS achieves tensile strength from 30 MPa to 45 MPa and elongation at break from 200% to 400%, providing a mechanical balance from rigidity and flexibility suitable for flexible packaging and agricultural film applications. The biodegradation rate of PBS reaches complete decomposition within 6 to 12 months under industrial composting conditions, degrading faster than PCL but slower than PLA under equivalent environmental conditions. PBS exhibits a density from 1.23 g/cm³ to 1.26 g/cm³ and a melt flow index from 1.5 g/10 min to 5.0 g/10 min, supporting processing through standard extrusion and injection molding equipment used in conventional thermoplastic manufacturing operations. 6. Engineering Plastics Engineering plastics are high-performance synthetic polymers that deliver superior mechanical strength, thermal stability, and chemical resistance beyond commodity plastics (polyethylene and polypropylene) in demanding structural and industrial applications. The types of engineering plastics are polycarbonate (PC), acrylonitrile butadiene styrene (ABS), polyoxymethylene (POM/Acetal), and polyether ether ketone (PEEK), each differentiated by molecular structure, thermal performance, and mechanical load capacity. Engineering plastics are processed through injection molding, extrusion, and machining at temperatures from 200°C to 400°C, depending on polymer type and grade. Tensile strength ranges from 40 MPa in standard ABS grades to over 100 MPa in PEEK and reinforced polycarbonate formulations, exceeding commodity thermoplastics at 15 MPa to 40 MPa. The heat deflection temperature spans from 80°C in standard ABS to over 300°C in high-performance PEEK formulations, reflecting the broad thermal range across the polymer class. The dimensional stability, creep resistance, and fatigue strength of engineering plastics position them as the preferred polymer class for precision mechanical components (gears, bearings, and structural housings) across automotive, aerospace, medical, and electronics manufacturing. Polycarbonate (PC) Polycarbonate is an amorphous engineering thermoplastic produced through the condensation polymerization of bisphenol-A (BPA) and phosgene, forming a transparent polymer with exceptional impact resistance and optical clarity. PC achieves tensile strength from 55 MPa to 75 MPa, impact resistance from 600 J/m to 850 J/m on the Izod notched test, and light transmittance of approximately 88%, making it a preferred glazing material in safety and optical applications. The heat deflection temperature of polycarbonate ranges from 120°C to 140°C, maintaining structural integrity under sustained thermal loading beyond standard thermoplastics. PC exhibits a refractive index of 1.586, making it suitable for precision optical lenses, eyewear, and light guide applications. The impact resistance, optical clarity, and thermal stability define the broad industrial performance of Polycarbonate (PC) across automotive glazing, electronics housings, and safety shield manufacturing. Acrylonitrile Butadiene Styrene (ABS) Acrylonitrile butadiene styrene is an amorphous engineering thermoplastic produced through the emulsion or bulk polymerization of three monomers, acrylonitrile (15% to 35%), butadiene (5% to 30%), and styrene (40% to 60%), forming a terpolymer with balanced rigidity, toughness, and surface finish quality. ABS achieves tensile strength from 40 MPa to 50 MPa, impact resistance from 100 J/m to 400 J/m on the Izod notched test, and a heat deflection temperature from 80°C to 100°C. The butadiene rubber phase dispersed within the styrene-acrylonitrile matrix absorbs impact energy, preventing brittle fracture under sudden mechanical loads. ABS exhibits a density of 1.01 g/cm³ to 1.21 g/cm³ and produces smooth, paintable surfaces suitable for consumer electronics housings, automotive interior trim, and 3D printing filament applications. The toughness, processability, and surface quality define the manufacturing versatility of Acrylonitrile Butadiene Styrene (ABS) . Polyoxymethylene (POM / Acetal) Polyoxymethylene is a semi-crystalline engineering thermoplastic produced through the polymerization of formaldehyde or trioxane, forming a highly ordered molecular structure with exceptional stiffness, dimensional stability, and low friction properties. POM achieves tensile strength from 60 MPa to 70 MPa, flexural modulus from 2,600 MPa to 3,100 MPa, and a melting point from 165°C to 175°C in homopolymer grades. The coefficient of friction of POM against steel measures from 0.1 to 0.3, making it the preferred engineering plastic for self-lubricating mechanical components (gears, bushings, and bearing surfaces) without external lubrication. POM exhibits a moisture absorption rate below 0.2% at equilibrium, maintaining dimensional accuracy in precision mechanical components exposed to humid operating environments. The stiffness, low friction, and dimensional stability of POM position it as the preferred material for high-precision mechanical components across automotive, consumer electronics, and industrial equipment manufacturing. Polyether Ether Ketone (PEEK) Polyether ether ketone is a semi-crystalline high-performance engineering thermoplastic produced through nucleophilic aromatic substitution polymerization, forming a polymer with a continuous service temperature from 250°C to 260°C and exceptional chemical resistance across aggressive industrial environments. PEEK achieves tensile strength from 90 MPa to 100 MPa in unfilled grades and up to 200 MPa in carbon fiber reinforced formulations, placing it among the highest-performing thermoplastics in commercial production. The flexural modulus of PEEK ranges from 3,600 MPa to 4,100 MPa in standard grades, with carbon fiber reinforced grades reaching 14,000 MPa for structural aerospace and medical implant applications. PEEK exhibits a chemical resistance profile covering concentrated acids, hydrocarbons, and organic solvents, maintaining mechanical integrity where standard engineering plastics degrade. The thermal stability, mechanical strength, and chemical resistance define the critical performance attributes of Polyether Ether Ketone (PEEK) across aerospace, medical, and semiconductor manufacturing. What Are the Uses of Synthetic Polymers? The uses of synthetic polymers are listed below. Packaging : Polyethylene, polypropylene, and PET dominate flexible and rigid packaging production across the food and consumer goods industries. Polyethylene film achieves oxygen permeability from 1,000 to 8,000 cm³/m²/day, providing moisture and gas barrier performance. Textile and Apparel : Polyester, nylon, and acrylic account for approximately 65% of global fiber production, replacing natural fibers in apparel and technical textile applications. Polyester fiber achieves tenacity from 3.5 g/d to 9.5 g/d across standard and high-tenacity grades. Automotive Components : Polycarbonate, ABS, and PEEK are used in instrument panels, bumper fascias, and structural housings, reducing component weight by 30% to 50% compared to metal parts. PEEK reinforced grades achieve tensile strength up to 200 MPa in under-hood applications. Medical Devices : P...

sections.heading: 6 Types of Synthetic Polymers
sections.text: 6 Types of Synthetic Polymers 6 Types of Synthetic Polymers

sections.heading: 1. Thermoplastics
sections.text: 1. Thermoplastics Thermoplastics are synthetic polymers that soften when heated and resolidify upon cooling, allowing repeated reshaping without chemical degradation of the polymer chain. The types of thermoplastics are polyethylene (PE), polypropylene (PP), polyvinyl chloride (PVC), polystyrene (PS), polyethylene terephthalate (PET), nylon, and acrylic (PMMA), each differentiated by molecular structure, thermal behavior, and mechanical performance. Thermoplastics are processed through injection molding, extrusion, and thermoforming at temperatures ranging from 150°C to 350°C, depending on polymer type and grade. The absence of cross-linking in thermoplastic molecular chains allows the material to be remelted and reprocessed multiple times without property loss. Thermoplastics achieve tensile strength from 15 MPa in low-density polyethylene (LDPE) to over 80 MPa in nylon and engineering-grade acrylic (PMMA). The softening point, measured as the heat deflection temperature (HDT), ranges from 50°C in low-density polyethylene to 140°C in polypropylene homopolymer grades. The combination of processability, mechanical versatility, and recyclability positions thermoplastics as the most...

sections.heading: Polyethylene (PE)
sections.text: Polyethylene (PE) Polyethylene is the most produced thermoplastic, synthesized through the polymerization of ethylene monomers (C₂H₄) into long-chain molecular structures ranging from low-density (LDPE) to high-density (HDPE) grades. LDPE achieves tensile strength from 8 MPa to 20 MPa, while HDPE reaches 21 MPa to 37 MPa. LDPE is characterized by a branched molecular structure that reduces crystallinity to 45% to 55%, producing a flexible, transparent film material. HDPE exhibits a linear molecular structure with crystallinity from 70% to 90%, generating a stiffer, more rigid material suitable for structural applications. LDPE is used in packaging films, squeeze bottles, and agricultural sheeting, while HDPE is applied in pipes, containers, and industrial tanks. Polyethylene resists moisture, dilute acids, and alkalis, maintaining chemical stability across a broad range of industrial and consumer Polyethylene (PE) applications.

sections.heading: Polypropylene (PP)
sections.text: Polypropylene (PP) Polypropylene is a semi-crystalline thermoplastic produced through the polymerization of propylene monomers (C₃H₆), achieving tensile strength from 25 MPa to 40 MPa and a heat deflection temperature from 100°C to 140°C. The polymer is produced in three primary tacticity forms (isotactic, syndiotactic, and atactic), with isotactic polypropylene accounting for the dominant share of commercial production due to its superior stiffness and thermal resistance. Polypropylene density ranges from 0.895 g/cm³ to 0.92 g/cm³, making it the lightest commodity thermoplastic in commercial production. Its fatigue resistance makes it the preferred material for living hinges, withstanding over 1,000,000 flex cycles without fracture. Polypropylene is applied in automotive components, food packaging containers, medical devices, and textile fiber production, where chemical resistance and thermal stability define the performance range of Polypropylene (PP) .

sections.heading: Polyvinyl Chloride (PVC)
sections.text: Polyvinyl Chloride (PVC) Polyvinyl chloride is a thermoplastic produced through the polymerization of vinyl chloride monomers (C₂H₃Cl), available in rigid and flexible formulations with tensile strength from 40 MPa to 60 MPa in rigid grades. Rigid PVC (uPVC) contains no plasticizer additives, producing a stiff material with a density of 1.3 g/cm³ to 1.45 g/cm³ used in pipe systems, window profiles, and building cladding. Flexible PVC is produced through the addition of plasticizers (dioctyl phthalate or diisononyl phthalate) at concentrations from 10% to 60% by weight, reducing stiffness for cable insulation, flooring, and medical tubing applications. PVC achieves a limiting oxygen index (LOI) from 45% to 49%, classifying it as a self-extinguishing material with inherent flame resistance. The rigid and flexible formulation range defines the broad industrial applicability of Polyvinyl Chloride (PVC) .

sections.heading: Polystyrene (PS)
sections.text: Polystyrene (PS) Polystyrene is an amorphous thermoplastic produced through the polymerization of styrene monomers (C₈H₈), achieving tensile strength from 25 MPa to 50 MPa in standard grades and up to 55 MPa in high-impact polystyrene (HIPS). Standard polystyrene exhibits a glass transition temperature of approximately 100°C, above which the material softens and loses structural rigidity. HIPS is produced by incorporating polybutadiene rubber into the polystyrene matrix at concentrations from 5% to 15%, increasing impact resistance at the cost of optical clarity. Expanded polystyrene (EPS) is produced by introducing a blowing agent during polymerization, generating a closed-cell foam structure with densities from 10 kg/m³ to 50 kg/m³ for thermal insulation applications. The range of standard, high-impact, and expanded grades defines the broad application spectrum of Polystyrene (PS) .

sections.heading: Polyethylene Terephthalate (PET)
sections.text: Polyethylene Terephthalate (PET) Polyethylene terephthalate is a semi-crystalline thermoplastic polyester produced through the condensation polymerization of ethylene glycol and terephthalic acid, achieving tensile strength from 50 MPa to 80 MPa. The crystallinity of PET ranges from 0% in amorphous grades to 60% in highly oriented fiber grades, with crystallinity directly influencing mechanical strength and barrier performance. PET exhibits an oxygen permeability from 0.05 to 0.1 cm³·mm/(m²·day·atm), making it the preferred barrier material for carbonated beverage bottles and food packaging. The intrinsic viscosity of PET, measured from 0.55 dL/g to 0.85 dL/g, determines suitability for bottle, film, or fiber applications, with higher viscosity grades used in structural fiber production. The barrier performance and mechanical range of PET define the material versatility of Polyethylene Terephthalate (PET) across the packaging and textile industries.

sections.heading: Nylon
sections.text: Nylon Nylon is a semi-crystalline polyamide thermoplastic produced through condensation polymerization, achieving tensile strength from 50 MPa to 85 MPa and a melting point from 215°C to 265°C, depending on grade. Nylon 6 is produced through ring-opening polymerization of caprolactam, while Nylon 6,6 is synthesized through the condensation of hexamethylenediamine and adipic acid, producing a polymer with slightly higher stiffness and thermal resistance. The moisture absorption of nylon ranges from 1.5% to 3.5% at equilibrium, reducing tensile strength and dimensional stability in high-humidity environments. Nylon exhibits a coefficient of friction from 0.15 to 0.40 against steel, making it suitable for self-lubricating gear, bearing, and bushing applications without external lubrication. The wear resistance and fatigue strength of nylon grades define the mechanical performance range of Nylon Types across industrial and textile applications.

sections.heading: Acrylic (PMMA)
sections.text: Acrylic (PMMA) Acrylic, or polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA), is an amorphous thermoplastic produced through the polymerization of methyl methacrylate monomers (C₅H₈O₂), achieving tensile strength from 50 MPa to 75 MPa and light transmittance of approximately 92%. The glass transition temperature of PMMA ranges from 85°C to 105°C, above which the material softens sufficiently for thermoforming and reshaping operations. PMMA exhibits a Vickers hardness from 18 HV to 20 HV, providing superior scratch resistance compared to polycarbonate at 14 HV to 16 HV. The refractive index of PMMA measures 1.49, closely matching optical glass and making it suitable for precision optical lenses, light guides, and display panel applications. The optical clarity, UV resistance, and dimensional stability of PMMA define the performance characteristics of Acrylic (PMMA) across signage, glazing, and medical device applications.

sections.heading: 2. Thermosetting Polymers (Thermosets)
sections.text: 2. Thermosetting Polymers (Thermosets) Thermosetting polymers are synthetic polymers that harden permanently after heating through an irreversible cross-linking reaction, forming a rigid three-dimensional molecular network that cannot be remelted or reshaped after curing. The types of thermosetting polymers are thermosetting epoxy resins, phenolic resins (Bakelite), melamine formaldehyde, urea formaldehyde, and polyester resins, each differentiated by curing mechanism, cross-link density, and mechanical performance. Thermosets are processed through compression molding, transfer molding, and resin infusion at curing temperatures from 120°C to 200°C, depending on resin system and hardener composition. The irreversible cross-linked network prevents molecular chain movement above the glass transition temperature, producing a dimensionally stable material that retains structural integrity under sustained thermal and mechanical loading. Thermosets achieve tensile strength from 40 MPa in urea formaldehyde to over 130 MPa in high-performance epoxy systems reinforced with carbon or glass fiber. The heat deflection temperature of thermosets ranges from 130°C in polyester resins to over 250°...

sections.heading: Epoxy Resins
sections.text: Epoxy Resins Epoxy resins are thermosetting polymers produced through the reaction of epichlorohydrin and bisphenol-A (BPA), forming a polymer with reactive epoxide groups that cure irreversibly upon exposure to hardeners (amines, anhydrides, or polyamides) at temperatures from 20°C to 200°C. The cured epoxy network achieves tensile strength from 55 MPa to 130 MPa, compressive strength from 100 MPa to 200 MPa, and a glass transition temperature from 120°C to 180°C, depending on hardener type and curing conditions. Epoxy resins exhibit excellent adhesion to metals, ceramics, and composite substrates, with bond shear strength from 10 MPa to 30 MPa in structural adhesive applications. The low shrinkage during curing, from 1% to 5% by volume, maintains dimensional accuracy in precision composite and tooling applications. The mechanical strength, chemical resistance, and adhesion performance define the broad industrial range of the epoxy definition .

sections.heading: Phenolic Resins (Bakelite)
sections.text: Phenolic Resins (Bakelite) Phenolic resins are thermosetting polymers produced through the condensation reaction of phenol and formaldehyde, forming a rigid cross-linked network that cures irreversibly under heat and pressure at temperatures from 150°C to 180°C. Bakelite, the first commercially produced synthetic polymer, introduced in 1907 by Leo Baekeland, remains the most recognized phenolic resin grade in industrial and consumer product history. Cured phenolic resins achieve tensile strength from 40 MPa to 70 MPa, compressive strength from 140 MPa to 210 MPa, and a heat deflection temperature from 150°C to 300°C, providing superior thermal stability among commodity thermosets. Phenolic resins exhibit a limiting oxygen index (LOI) from 25% to 35%, classifying them as inherently flame-resistant materials suitable for electrical components and fire-rated construction panels. The thermal stability and flame resistance define the industrial performance of phenolic resins .

sections.heading: Melamine Formaldehyde
sections.text: Melamine Formaldehyde Melamine formaldehyde is a thermosetting polymer produced through the condensation reaction of melamine and formaldehyde, forming a hard, rigid cross-linked network with superior surface hardness and scratch resistance compared to other amino resins. The cured polymer achieves tensile strength from 50 MPa to 80 MPa, compressive strength from 200 MPa to 300 MPa, and a heat deflection temperature from 130°C to 200°C, maintaining structural integrity under sustained thermal loading. Melamine formaldehyde exhibits a Brinell hardness from 25 HB to 40 HB, producing a surface resistant to abrasion, staining, and moisture penetration in decorative laminate and tableware applications. The material resists dilute acids and alkalis, maintaining surface integrity across food contact and chemical exposure conditions. Melamine formaldehyde is applied in decorative laminates, kitchenware, electrical components, and fire-retardant coatings across consumer and industrial product manufacturing.

sections.heading: Urea Formaldehyde
sections.text: Urea Formaldehyde Urea formaldehyde is a thermosetting polymer produced through the condensation reaction of urea and formaldehyde, forming a rigid, colorless cross-linked network cured at temperatures from 100°C to 150°C under pressure. The cured polymer achieves tensile strength from 38 MPa to 55 MPa, compressive strength from 170 MPa to 230 MPa, and a heat deflection temperature from 120°C to 145°C, providing moderate thermal resistance for indoor applications. Urea formaldehyde exhibits superior hardness and surface finish quality, making it a preferred binder resin in particleboard, medium-density fiberboard (MDF), and decorative paper laminates at resin loading levels from 8% to 15% by weight. The material is susceptible to hydrolysis under prolonged moisture exposure, limiting its application to interior environments. Urea formaldehyde is applied in wood adhesives, electrical switch housings, and molded consumer product components.

sections.heading: Polyester Resins
sections.text: Polyester Resins Polyester resins are thermosetting polymers produced through the condensation polymerization of diols and dicarboxylic acids, dissolved in styrene monomer at concentrations from 30% to 50% by weight to form a liquid resin system that cures through free-radical cross-linking at room temperature or elevated temperatures. Unsaturated polyester resins (UPR) achieve tensile strength from 40 MPa to 90 MPa and a glass transition temperature from 70°C to 120°C, depending on resin formulation and reinforcement type. Orthophthalic polyester resins portray the standard grade, while isophthalic polyester resins provide superior corrosion resistance and mechanical performance for marine and chemical processing applications. Polyester resins exhibit volumetric shrinkage from 4% to 8% during curing, requiring careful mold design to maintain dimensional accuracy in composite part production. The cost-effectiveness and processing versatility define the broad application range of polyester definition across marine, automotive, and construction composite manufacturing.

sections.heading: 3. Elastomers
sections.text: 3. Elastomers Elastomers are flexible, rubber-like synthetic polymers that stretch under applied force and return to their original shape upon load removal, a property governed by a lightly cross-linked molecular network that allows large reversible deformation. The types of elastomers are natural rubber, synthetic rubber, neoprene, silicone rubber, and polyurethane elastomers, each differentiated by chemical composition, cross-link density, and mechanical recovery performance. Elastomers are processed through vulcanization, compression molding, and extrusion at temperatures from 140°C to 200°C, with cross-link density controlling the balance between elastic recovery and stiffness across different grades. The elongation at break of elastomers ranges from 100% to over 800%, reflecting the exceptionally high deformation capacity that distinguishes them from rigid thermoplastics and thermosets. Elastomers achieve tensile strength from 10 MPa in standard synthetic rubber to 30 MPa in high-performance silicone and polyurethane grades. The service temperature range spans from 60°C in low-temperature silicone grades to 230°C in high-temperature silicone formulations, positioning elastome...

sections.heading: Natural Rubber
sections.text: Natural Rubber Natural rubber is an elastomer derived from the latex sap of the Hevea brasiliensis tree, composed of cis-1,4-polyisoprene chains with a molecular weight ranging from 100,000 g/mol to 1,000,000 g/mol. The raw latex is harvested through bark tapping, then processed through coagulation, drying, and vulcanization using sulfur at concentrations from 1% to 3% by weight to form cross-linked networks that improve mechanical performance. Vulcanized natural rubber achieves tensile strength from 25 MPa to 35 MPa, elongation at break from 500% to 800%, and a service temperature range from -50°C to 80°C. Natural rubber exhibits superior resilience and low heat buildup under dynamic loading, making it the preferred elastomer for high-performance tire treads, industrial conveyor belts, and vibration isolation mounts requiring consistent elastic recovery, defining its role as a foundational natural rubber elastomer material.

sections.heading: Synthetic Rubber
sections.text: Synthetic Rubber Synthetic rubber is a petrochemical-derived elastomer produced through the polymerization of monomers (styrene, butadiene, isoprene, and chloroprene) to replicate and extend the mechanical properties of natural rubber across industrial applications. Styrene-butadiene rubber (SBR), the most widely produced synthetic rubber grade, is composed of 23% to 25% styrene and 75% to 77% butadiene by weight, achieving tensile strength from 15 MPa to 25 MPa in carbon-black reinforced compounds. Synthetic rubber exhibits superior aging resistance, ozone resistance, and chemical stability compared to natural rubber, extending service life in outdoor and chemically aggressive environments. The service temperature range of synthetic rubber grades spans from -50°C to 120°C, depending on polymer type and compounding formulation. Synthetic rubber is applied in tire treads, conveyor belts, seals, hoses, and industrial gaskets, reinforcing its dominance as a synthetic rubber elastomer across high-volume manufacturing.

sections.heading: Neoprene
sections.text: Neoprene Neoprene is a synthetic elastomer produced through the free-radical polymerization of chloroprene monomers (C₄H₅Cl), forming a polychloroprene polymer with a chlorine content of approximately 40% by weight that provides inherent flame and chemical resistance. Vulcanized neoprene achieves tensile strength from 15 MPa to 25 MPa, elongation at break from 300% to 600%, and a service temperature range from -40°C to 120°C, maintaining flexibility across wide thermal fluctuations. Neoprene exhibits superior resistance to oils, ozone, weathering, and moderate concentrations of acids and alkalis, outperforming natural rubber in chemically aggressive environments. The flame resistance of neoprene, with a limiting oxygen index (LOI) from 26% to 28%, makes it preferable for cable jacketing and fire-rated sealing applications. The chemical resistance and thermal stability of neoprene distinguish it from silicone rubber in the silicone vs. neoprene elastomer comparison.

sections.heading: Silicone Rubber
sections.text: Silicone Rubber Silicone rubber is an inorganic-organic elastomer produced through the polymerization of siloxane monomers (Si-O backbone), forming a polymer chain with methyl, vinyl, or phenyl side groups that govern thermal stability and mechanical performance across a service temperature range from -60°C to 230°C. Vulcanized silicone rubber achieves tensile strength from 5 MPa to 14 MPa, elongation at break from 100% to 700%, and a Shore A hardness from 10 to 80, depending on formulation and cross-link density. Silicone rubber exhibits superior biocompatibility, electrical insulation, and UV resistance compared to organic elastomers, maintaining mechanical properties across repeated thermal cycling. The dielectric strength of silicone rubber ranges from 15 kV/mm to 25 kV/mm, making it the preferred elastomer for high-voltage electrical insulation and medical implant applications, defining the performance scope of silicone rubber .

sections.heading: Polyurethane Elastomers
sections.text: Polyurethane Elastomers Polyurethane elastomers are synthetic elastomers produced through the reaction of polyols and diisocyanates, forming a segmented block copolymer structure with alternating hard and soft segments that govern mechanical performance and elastic recovery. Otto Bayer first synthesized polyurethane in 1937 at IG Farben laboratories in Germany, establishing the foundation for a polymer class that expanded into elastomers, foams, and coatings across industrial and consumer applications. Polyurethane elastomers achieve tensile strength from 20 MPa to 70 MPa, elongation at break from 300% to 600%, and Shore A hardness from 40 to 98, providing a broader mechanical range than natural rubber or neoprene. The abrasion resistance of polyurethane elastomers exceeds that of natural rubber by 3 to 5 times under standardized DIN 53516 testing conditions. The mechanical range and abrasion resistance define the industrial applications of polyurethane history across wheels, seals, and mining equipment components.

sections.heading: 4. Synthetic Fibers
sections.text: 4. Synthetic Fibers Synthetic fibers are strong, lightweight polymer strands produced through the extrusion of petrochemical-derived polymer solutions or melts through spinnerets, engineered to deliver specific tensile, thermal, and moisture management properties across textile and industrial applications. The types of synthetic fibers are nylon, polyester, acrylic fiber, spandex (Lycra), and rayon (semi-synthetic), each differentiated by polymer composition, fiber structure, and performance characteristics in apparel, home textiles, and technical fabric applications. Synthetic fibers are produced through melt spinning, wet spinning, or dry spinning processes at extrusion temperatures from 220°C to 290°C, depending on polymer type and target fiber denier. The tenacity of synthetic fibers ranges from 2 grams per denier (g/d) in standard acrylic to over 9 g/d in high-tenacity polyester and nylon grades. Synthetic fibers achieve moisture regain values from 0.4% in polyester to 4.5% in nylon, directly influencing drying performance and comfort in apparel applications. The tensile strength of synthetic fiber yarns ranges from 300 MPa in standard acrylic to over 1,000 MPa in high-tenaci...

sections.heading: Polyester
sections.text: Polyester Polyester is a semi-crystalline synthetic fiber produced through the condensation polymerization of ethylene glycol and terephthalic acid, forming polyethylene terephthalate (PET) fiber with tenacity from 3.5 g/d to 9.5 g/d in standard and high-tenacity grades. The moisture regain of polyester fiber is approximately 0.4% under standard atmospheric conditions, resulting in fast-drying performance in sportswear, outdoor apparel, and technical textile applications. Polyester fiber exhibits a melting point from 250°C to 265°C and a glass transition temperature from 70°C to 80°C, maintaining dimensional stability under repeated laundering at temperatures up to 60°C. The fiber resists stretching, shrinkage, and most mineral acids, maintaining tensile integrity across prolonged mechanical and chemical exposure. Polyester accounts for approximately 54% of global fiber production, making it the most widely manufactured synthetic fiber across apparel, home textiles, and industrial fabric applications.

sections.heading: Acrylic Fiber
sections.text: Acrylic Fiber Acrylic fiber is a synthetic textile fiber produced from polyacrylonitrile (PAN), a polymer composed of at least 85% acrylonitrile monomer by weight as defined by the U.S. Federal Trade Commission, with the remaining composition consisting of co-monomers (vinyl acetate or methyl acrylate) at concentrations from 5% to 15%. The fiber achieves tenacity from 2 g/d to 3.5 g/d, with a moisture regain of 1% to 2% at standard atmospheric conditions, enabling faster drying performance compared to wool at 17% moisture regain. Acrylic fiber density measures 1.17 g/cm³ to 1.18 g/cm³, placing it among the lightest synthetic fibers in commercial textile production. The crimped fiber structure traps air within the textile matrix, generating thermal insulation comparable to wool at lower fiber weight. The lightweight structure and wool-like thermal performance define the application range of acrylic fiber across cold-weather apparel and home textile markets.

sections.heading: Spandex (Lycra)
sections.text: Spandex (Lycra) Spandex, marketed under the trade name Lycra, is a synthetic elastomeric fiber produced from segmented polyurethane polymer chains composed of alternating hard and soft segments, achieving elongation at break from 400% to 700% with full elastic recovery upon load removal. The fiber is produced through dry spinning of dimethylformamide (DMF) dissolved polyurethane solution at extrusion temperatures from 120°C to 180°C, forming continuous filaments at deniers from 10 to 2,500 depending on application requirements. Spandex achieves tenacity from 0.6 g/d to 0.9 g/d, lower than nylon or polyester, but delivers unmatched elastic recovery performance across repeated stretch cycles. The moisture regain of spandex measures approximately 1.3% at standard conditions, limiting its moisture management capacity in high-intensity athletic applications. Spandex is applied in swimwear, activewear, shapewear, and compression garments where stretch recovery from 400% to 700% is required.

sections.heading: Rayon (Semi-synthetic)
sections.text: Rayon (Semi-synthetic) Rayon is a semi-synthetic fiber produced from regenerated cellulose derived from wood pulp or cotton linters, processed through chemical dissolution and wet spinning to form a fiber that bridges natural and fully synthetic textile materials. The cellulose source is dissolved in sodium hydroxide and carbon disulfide to form a viscose solution, then extruded through spinnerets into an acid coagulation bath at sulfuric acid concentrations from 10% to 15%, regenerating cellulose as continuous filaments. Rayon achieves tenacity from 1.5 g/d to 3.0 g/d in standard viscose grades and up to 6.9 g/d in high-tenacity modal and lyocell variants. The moisture regain of rayon ranges from 11% to 13% at standard atmospheric conditions, exceeding cotton at 8% and producing a highly absorbent, breathable fiber suitable for apparel and hygiene product applications. Rayon is applied in apparel linings, medical dressings, and nonwoven hygiene fabrics across consumer and industrial textile markets.

sections.heading: 5. Biodegradable Synthetic Polymers
sections.text: 5. Biodegradable Synthetic Polymers Biodegradable synthetic polymers are engineered polymer materials that break down through microbial activity, hydrolysis, or enzymatic degradation under specific environmental conditions, reducing long-term plastic accumulation in landfills and marine environments. The types of biodegradable synthetic polymers are polylactic acid (PLA), polycaprolactone (PCL), and polybutylene succinate (PBS), each differentiated by degradation rate, mechanical performance, and target application. Biodegradable synthetic polymers are processed through injection molding, extrusion, and film blowing at temperatures from 150°C to 220°C, depending on polymer type and molecular weight. Tensile strength ranges from 20 MPa in flexible PCL grades to 60 MPa in rigid PLA formulations, covering a mechanical range suitable for packaging, medical, and agricultural film applications. The glass transition temperature spans from 60°C in PCL to 60°C in standard PLA grades, reflecting the broad thermal performance spectrum across the polymer class. The degradation rate ranges from 6 months under industrial composting conditions to years in ambient soil environments, positioning b...

sections.heading: Polylactic Acid (PLA)
sections.text: Polylactic Acid (PLA) Polylactic acid is a biodegradable thermoplastic polyester produced through the ring-opening polymerization of lactide, a cyclic diester derived from lactic acid fermentation of renewable carbohydrate sources (corn starch, sugarcane, and cassava). PLA achieves tensile strength from 50 MPa to 70 MPa, a glass transition temperature from 55°C to 60°C, and a melting point from 150°C to 180°C, providing mechanical properties comparable to polystyrene in rigid packaging applications. The biodegradation rate of PLA reaches 60% to 80% decomposition within 60 to 90 days under industrial composting conditions at temperatures above 58°C and relative humidity above 50%. PLA exhibits a molecular weight from 100,000 g/mol to 300,000 g/mol, directly influencing mechanical strength and processing behavior during extrusion and injection molding. The renewable feedstock origin and compostability define the sustainability profile of Polylactic Acid (PLA) across packaging, medical implant, and agricultural film applications.

sections.heading: Polycaprolactone (PCL)
sections.text: Polycaprolactone (PCL) Polycaprolactone is a biodegradable semi-crystalline polyester produced through the ring-opening polymerization of ε-caprolactone monomer, forming a flexible, low-melting polymer with a melting point from 59°C to 64°C and a glass transition temperature of approximately -60°C. PCL achieves tensile strength from 20 MPa to 42 MPa and elongation at break from 300% to 1,000%, providing exceptional flexibility compared to rigid biodegradable polymers (PLA and PBS). The biodegradation rate of PCL is slower than that of PLA, requiring 2 to 4 years for complete degradation in soil environments through hydrolytic and enzymatic chain scission. PCL molecular weight ranges from 10,000 g/mol to 100,000 g/mol, with higher molecular weight grades delivering greater mechanical strength and slower degradation rates. The flexibility, biocompatibility, and controlled degradation rate define the medical and tissue engineering applications of Polycaprolactone (PCL) in sutures, drug delivery systems, and scaffold fabrication.

sections.heading: Polybutylene Succinate (PBS)
sections.text: Polybutylene Succinate (PBS) Polybutylene succinate is a biodegradable semi-crystalline aliphatic polyester produced through the condensation polymerization of succinic acid and 1,4-butanediol, forming a thermoplastic polymer with a melting point from 113°C to 115°C and a glass transition temperature of approximately -32°C. PBS achieves tensile strength from 30 MPa to 45 MPa and elongation at break from 200% to 400%, providing a mechanical balance from rigidity and flexibility suitable for flexible packaging and agricultural film applications. The biodegradation rate of PBS reaches complete decomposition within 6 to 12 months under industrial composting conditions, degrading faster than PCL but slower than PLA under equivalent environmental conditions. PBS exhibits a density from 1.23 g/cm³ to 1.26 g/cm³ and a melt flow index from 1.5 g/10 min to 5.0 g/10 min, supporting processing through standard extrusion and injection molding equipment used in conventional thermoplastic manufacturing operations.

sections.heading: 6. Engineering Plastics
sections.text: 6. Engineering Plastics Engineering plastics are high-performance synthetic polymers that deliver superior mechanical strength, thermal stability, and chemical resistance beyond commodity plastics (polyethylene and polypropylene) in demanding structural and industrial applications. The types of engineering plastics are polycarbonate (PC), acrylonitrile butadiene styrene (ABS), polyoxymethylene (POM/Acetal), and polyether ether ketone (PEEK), each differentiated by molecular structure, thermal performance, and mechanical load capacity. Engineering plastics are processed through injection molding, extrusion, and machining at temperatures from 200°C to 400°C, depending on polymer type and grade. Tensile strength ranges from 40 MPa in standard ABS grades to over 100 MPa in PEEK and reinforced polycarbonate formulations, exceeding commodity thermoplastics at 15 MPa to 40 MPa. The heat deflection temperature spans from 80°C in standard ABS to over 300°C in high-performance PEEK formulations, reflecting the broad thermal range across the polymer class. The dimensional stability, creep resistance, and fatigue strength of engineering plastics position them as the preferred polymer class fo...

sections.heading: Polycarbonate (PC)
sections.text: Polycarbonate (PC) Polycarbonate is an amorphous engineering thermoplastic produced through the condensation polymerization of bisphenol-A (BPA) and phosgene, forming a transparent polymer with exceptional impact resistance and optical clarity. PC achieves tensile strength from 55 MPa to 75 MPa, impact resistance from 600 J/m to 850 J/m on the Izod notched test, and light transmittance of approximately 88%, making it a preferred glazing material in safety and optical applications. The heat deflection temperature of polycarbonate ranges from 120°C to 140°C, maintaining structural integrity under sustained thermal loading beyond standard thermoplastics. PC exhibits a refractive index of 1.586, making it suitable for precision optical lenses, eyewear, and light guide applications. The impact resistance, optical clarity, and thermal stability define the broad industrial performance of Polycarbonate (PC) across automotive glazing, electronics housings, and safety shield manufacturing.

sections.heading: Acrylonitrile Butadiene Styrene (ABS)
sections.text: Acrylonitrile Butadiene Styrene (ABS) Acrylonitrile butadiene styrene is an amorphous engineering thermoplastic produced through the emulsion or bulk polymerization of three monomers, acrylonitrile (15% to 35%), butadiene (5% to 30%), and styrene (40% to 60%), forming a terpolymer with balanced rigidity, toughness, and surface finish quality. ABS achieves tensile strength from 40 MPa to 50 MPa, impact resistance from 100 J/m to 400 J/m on the Izod notched test, and a heat deflection temperature from 80°C to 100°C. The butadiene rubber phase dispersed within the styrene-acrylonitrile matrix absorbs impact energy, preventing brittle fracture under sudden mechanical loads. ABS exhibits a density of 1.01 g/cm³ to 1.21 g/cm³ and produces smooth, paintable surfaces suitable for consumer electronics housings, automotive interior trim, and 3D printing filament applications. The toughness, processability, and surface quality define the manufacturing versatility of Acrylonitrile Butadiene Styrene (ABS) .

sections.heading: Polyoxymethylene (POM / Acetal)
sections.text: Polyoxymethylene (POM / Acetal) Polyoxymethylene is a semi-crystalline engineering thermoplastic produced through the polymerization of formaldehyde or trioxane, forming a highly ordered molecular structure with exceptional stiffness, dimensional stability, and low friction properties. POM achieves tensile strength from 60 MPa to 70 MPa, flexural modulus from 2,600 MPa to 3,100 MPa, and a melting point from 165°C to 175°C in homopolymer grades. The coefficient of friction of POM against steel measures from 0.1 to 0.3, making it the preferred engineering plastic for self-lubricating mechanical components (gears, bushings, and bearing surfaces) without external lubrication. POM exhibits a moisture absorption rate below 0.2% at equilibrium, maintaining dimensional accuracy in precision mechanical components exposed to humid operating environments. The stiffness, low friction, and dimensional stability of POM position it as the preferred material for high-precision mechanical components across automotive, consumer electronics, and industrial equipment manufacturing.

sections.heading: Polyether Ether Ketone (PEEK)
sections.text: Polyether Ether Ketone (PEEK) Polyether ether ketone is a semi-crystalline high-performance engineering thermoplastic produced through nucleophilic aromatic substitution polymerization, forming a polymer with a continuous service temperature from 250°C to 260°C and exceptional chemical resistance across aggressive industrial environments. PEEK achieves tensile strength from 90 MPa to 100 MPa in unfilled grades and up to 200 MPa in carbon fiber reinforced formulations, placing it among the highest-performing thermoplastics in commercial production. The flexural modulus of PEEK ranges from 3,600 MPa to 4,100 MPa in standard grades, with carbon fiber reinforced grades reaching 14,000 MPa for structural aerospace and medical implant applications. PEEK exhibits a chemical resistance profile covering concentrated acids, hydrocarbons, and organic solvents, maintaining mechanical integrity where standard engineering plastics degrade. The thermal stability, mechanical strength, and chemical resistance define the critical performance attributes of Polyether Ether Ketone (PEEK) across aerospace, medical, and semiconductor manufacturing.

sections.heading: What Are the Uses of Synthetic Polymers?
sections.text: What Are the Uses of Synthetic Polymers? The uses of synthetic polymers are listed below. Packaging : Polyethylene, polypropylene, and PET dominate flexible and rigid packaging production across the food and consumer goods industries. Polyethylene film achieves oxygen permeability from 1,000 to 8,000 cm³/m²/day, providing moisture and gas barrier performance. Textile and Apparel : Polyester, nylon, and acrylic account for approximately 65% of global fiber production, replacing natural fibers in apparel and technical textile applications. Polyester fiber achieves tenacity from 3.5 g/d to 9.5 g/d across standard and high-tenacity grades. Automotive Components : Polycarbonate, ABS, and PEEK are used in instrument panels, bumper fascias, and structural housings, reducing component weight by 30% to 50% compared to metal parts. PEEK reinforced grades achieve tensile strength up to 200 MPa in under-hood applications. Medical Devices : PEEK, polycarbonate, and PLA are used in surgical implants, drug delivery systems, and medical device housings requiring sterilization resistance. text_excerpt: Resources / Materials / 6 Types of Synthetic Polymers 6 Types of Synthetic Polymers Written by Megan Conniff Updated by Audrius Zidonis PhD 28 min read Published November 25, 2026 The 6 types of synthetic polymers are thermoplastics, thermosetting polymers (thermosets), elastomers, synthetic fibers, biodegradable synthetic polymers, and engineering plastics, each classified by molecular structure, thermal behavior, and mechanical performance. Synthetic polymers are large-chain molecules produced through polymerization of monomer units derived from petrochemical feedstocks, engineered to deliver specific physical and chemical properties across industrial and consumer applications. Thermoplastics (polyethylene and polypropylene) soften upon heating and resolidify upon cooling, while thermosets (epoxy and phenolic resins) cure irreversibly through cross-linking. Elastomers (silicone and styrene-butadiene rubber) exhibit high elastic recovery, and synthetic fibers (nylon and polyester) provide tensile strength in textile applications.
